title: Mouth-moistening and lip care after drinking becomes hard

source_packet.source_basis: Public-source practice-layer synthesis for schema testing; no private testimony, no contributor interview, no claim of corpus completeness.
limitations: Public sources describe recognized care patterns but do not supply firsthand room texture.
This record must not become procedure-level instruction for a particular death.
Treatment, legal, ritual, emergency, and equipment decisions remain local and must be handled by qualified teams or relevant authorities.

moment.plain_scene: The person’s mouth and lips look dry, drinking is difficult or unsafe, and carers look for small comfort practices: moistening, lip care, and asking the care team what is safe.
ordinary_language_queries: dry mouth dying what can I do

content_layers.observation_text: Public sources distinguish the comfort problem of a dry mouth from the medical question of hydration; professional mouth-care guidance emphasizes assessment, safety, positioning, moistening, and care-team direction.
content_layers.source_synthesis: Marie Curie professional guidance supports mouth assessment and mouth-moistening practices under appropriate review; Hospice UK and healthdirect provide family-facing orientation.

interpretation.editor_interpretation: This record turns mouth care from a throwaway note into a core bedside craft lane: love moves from glass of water to careful comfort, without shaming the impulse to give water.

what_this_is_not: not permission to put fluid in the mouth when swallowing is unsafe
not a procedural manual for swabs, syringes, sprays, or suction
not a substitute for nursing, hospice, or speech/swallowing assessment
uncertainties: The safe boundary for sips, ice, swabs, gels, or sprays depends on local assessment.
Products and practices vary by setting.
Some cultural or family meanings of water at death need separate tradition-governed records.
content_layers.lay_orientation: A lay surface should translate “mouth care” as comfort for lips and mouth, while routing swallowing or fluid questions back to the care team.
content_layers.practitioner_notes: A practitioner surface should collect explanation scripts and demonstration boundaries: what can be shown safely, what must be assessed, and how to reduce guilt around not giving a drink.
language_notes: Avoid framing dry mouth as neglect.
Route “thirst” searches to careful explanation, not certainty.

provenance.provenance_statement: Drafted from named public sources to test the practice layer. It should be reviewed before any public surface uses it.

safety.clinical_boundary: This record is observational/source-indexing only. It is not medical advice, not a prognosis, not a legal instruction, not a ritual authority, and not a substitute for a local hospice, clinician, emergency, legal, cultural, or care team.
safety.safety_notes: Before public use, route through clinical or domain review and ensure any lay surface directs urgent, worried, legal, medication, swallowing, equipment, or body-handling questions to qualified local support.
